name: Simulated Clinical Trials
title: Simulated Clinical Trials
answer: Simulated clinical trials use computational models of disease, drug action and patient populations to test whether a treatment is likely to work before or alongside human studies. They sit within drug discovery and molecular simulation, where the same physics and statistics that describe a molecule binding to a protein are scaled up to describe a whole trial. The scope covers trial design, dose selection, patient subgroup analysis and the prediction of adverse events, and it draws on real trial data, electronic health records and mechanistic models of the body. It does not replace a real trial, it narrows the space of candidates and questions that a real trial has to answer.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Simulated clinical trials use computational models of disease, drug action and patient populations to test whether a treatment is likely to work before or alongside human studies. They sit within drug discovery and molecular simulation, where the same physics and statistics that describe a molecule binding to a protein are scaled up to describe a whole trial. The scope covers trial design, dose selection, patient subgroup analysis and the prediction of adverse events, and it draws on real trial data, electronic health records and mechanistic models of the body. It does not replace a real trial, it narrows the space of candidates and questions that a real trial has to answer.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on high performance computing clusters and cloud GPU instances, because a single simulation can involve thousands of virtual patients followed over months of modelled time. Molecular dynamics engines, ordinary differential equation solvers and agent based simulation frameworks sit under the hood, with data pipelines pulling from trial databases and clinical registries. The site tracks 804 scientific models, a reminder that most of these systems are specialised rather than general. Storage and compute costs scale with the number of virtual patients and the granularity of the physiological model, so teams trade resolution against throughput.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical study starts by building a model of the disease course and the drug's mechanism, then calibrating it against published trial results or patient level data. Virtual patients are sampled from distributions that reflect real variation in age, weight, genetics and comorbidity, and each is run through the model under different doses and schedules. Sensitivity analysis shows which assumptions drive the outcome, and the results are compared against historical trials to check that the model reproduces what was already known. Teams then use the simulation to rank candidate designs before committing to a costly human study.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Regulators treat simulated evidence as supporting material rather than a substitute for clinical data, and submissions that lean on it must document the model, its assumptions and its validation. Provenance matters: the source of every input dataset, the version of the model and the code that ran it need to be traceable, because a result that cannot be reproduced cannot be defended. The site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows how quickly a modelling claim can become a legal question. Privacy rules apply to any real patient data used for calibration, and consent and data use agreements govern how that data moves between parties.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward models that are validated prospectively, meaning their predictions are registered before the real trial reads out and then scored against it. That requires shared benchmarks, common data standards and a way to certify a model the way a laboratory assay is certified. Digital twins of individual patients, built from their own records, are an active area, though the evidence base is still thin. As simulated evidence becomes more routine in submissions, the pressure will fall on transparency and on keeping the boundary between prediction and proof clear.
